gloss: A seat for one person, usually with a back and four legs.
examples: Pull up a *chair* and sit with us.
We need two more *chairs* for the dinner table.
He tipped his *chair* back and put his feet up.

gloss: A piece of furniture with a flat top on legs.
examples: Set the *table* — dinner's almost ready.
All the *tables* by the window were taken.
She left her keys on the kitchen *table*.

gloss: A low table placed in front of a sofa.
examples: There were magazines stacked all over the *coffee table*.
We found a *coffee table* at a yard sale for twenty bucks.
The kids kept banging their heads on the *coffee table*.

gloss: A table for writing, reading, or working at a computer.
examples: My *desk* is buried under paperwork.
The classroom had thirty *desks* in neat rows.
She keeps a photo of her kids on her *desk*.

gloss: A long padded seat for two or more people.
examples: The cat sheds all over the *sofa*.
They're looking at *sofas* for the new apartment.
He fell asleep on the *sofa* watching the game.

gloss: A sofa; the usual everyday word for one in American homes.
examples: You can crash on the *couch* if it's too late to drive.
We moved both *couches* to get the rug underneath.
There's about four dollars in change under the *couch* cushions.

gloss: A comfortable chair with supports for the arms.
examples: Grandpa always sat in the same *armchair* by the fire.
The two *armchairs* face each other across the rug.
She curled up in the *armchair* with a book.

gloss: A chair on curved runners that rocks back and forth.
examples: She rocked the baby to sleep in the old *rocking chair*.
There are two *rocking chairs* out on the front porch.
The *rocking chair* creaks every time you lean back.

gloss: A backless seat, often tall enough for a counter or bar.
examples: He sat on a *stool* at the end of the bar.
We bought three *stools* for the kitchen island.
Stand on the *stool* if you can't reach the top shelf.

gloss: A long seat for several people, usually without a back.
examples: We ate lunch on a *bench* in the park.
The *benches* in the hallway were bolted to the wall.
There's a storage *bench* by the back door for shoes.

gloss: An armchair whose back tilts and whose footrest lifts up.
examples: Dad claimed the *recliner* the second he walked in.
The theater has heated *recliners* now.
He leaned the *recliner* all the way back and dozed off.

gloss: A small sofa built for exactly two people.
examples: The apartment's too small for a full couch, so we got a *loveseat*.
Both *loveseats* were on clearance.
She sat on the *loveseat* across from the window.

gloss: A low padded seat with no back, often used as a footrest.
examples: Put your feet up on the *ottoman*.
The *ottoman* opens up and there's storage inside.
They use two small *ottomans* instead of a coffee table.

gloss: The part of a chair you sit on, or a place to sit.
examples: The *seat* on that chair is starting to sag.
Save me a *seat* if you get there first.
All the good *seats* were gone by seven.

gloss: A soft padded bag used to sit on or lean against.
examples: I found the remote under a *cushion*.
The couch *cushions* need to be flipped.
She propped a *cushion* behind her back.

gloss: A tall chair with a tray where a baby sits to eat.
examples: Can we get a *highchair* for the baby?
He threw half his dinner off the *highchair*.
The restaurant only had two *highchairs*.

gloss: A narrow table that stands against a wall.
examples: We keep the mail in a basket on the hall *console*.
A pair of lamps sits on the *console* behind the sofa.
Both *consoles* were too deep for that narrow hallway.
contrast: Stress shifts between the noun and the verb: the table is a KAHN-sohl, but to comfort someone is kuhn-SOHL.

gloss: A piece of furniture you sleep on.
examples: Make your *bed* before you leave.
The room has two twin *beds*.
I was still in *bed* when he called.

gloss: The thick padded pad you lie on, resting on a bed frame.
examples: This *mattress* is way too soft for my back.
They deliver the *mattress* on Saturday.
We flip the *mattresses* twice a year.

gloss: The upright panel at the head end of a bed.
examples: She leaned against the *headboard* and read for a while.
The bed came without a *headboard*.
They make *headboards* out of old barn wood.

gloss: Two beds built one above the other.
examples: The boys share a *bunk bed*.
I always called top on the *bunk bed*.
The cabins have four *bunk beds* each.

gloss: A baby's bed with high barred sides.
examples: He finally fell asleep in his *crib*.
We're assembling the *crib* this weekend.
Older *cribs* don't meet the current safety rules.
contrast: American *crib* is British *cot* — and an American *cot* is something else entirely.

gloss: A light folding bed, easy to set up and put away.
examples: We put a *cot* in the office for guests.
The shelter set up a hundred *cots* in the gym.
A *cot* is fine — I can sleep anywhere.
contrast: In American English a *cot* is a folding camp bed; in British English it means a baby's crib.

gloss: A small bed for a newborn that rocks from side to side.
examples: The baby slept in a *cradle* beside their bed.
He carved the *cradle* himself.
Antique *cradles* sell for a lot at auction.

gloss: A padded mattress on a frame that folds out from a couch into a bed.
examples: I slept on their *futon* for three months.
The *futon* folds flat in about ten seconds.
College apartments are full of secondhand *futons*.

gloss: A hanging bed of cloth or netting slung between two supports.
examples: He spent the whole afternoon in the *hammock*.
We strung a *hammock* between two trees.
The porch has two *hammocks* and not much else.

gloss: A small table next to a bed.
examples: My glasses are on the *nightstand*.
There's a matching *nightstand* on each side of the bed.
She keeps a glass of water and a book on her *nightstand*.
contrast: The *gh* is silent, exactly as in *night*: NYT-stand.

gloss: A low chest of drawers for clothes, usually in a bedroom.
examples: Your socks are in the top drawer of the *dresser*.
We refinished an old *dresser* we found at a thrift store.
Both *dressers* are too big for that room.
contrast: American *dresser* is British *chest of drawers*.

gloss: A tall freestanding cupboard for hanging clothes.
examples: The old house has no closets, just a *wardrobe* in each room.
They hauled the *wardrobe* up two flights of stairs.
Antique *wardrobes* barely fit through modern doorways.
contrast: In the US a *wardrobe* is a freestanding piece of furniture; built-in storage in the wall is a *closet*.

gloss: A large ornate cabinet for clothes or a television.
examples: The TV is hidden inside that *armoire*.
She inherited a walnut *armoire* from her grandmother.
Two *armoires* took up most of the bedroom.
contrast: A French borrowing: *-oire* is said /wɑːr/, so it ends like the word *war*.

gloss: A dressing table with a mirror, or a bathroom cabinet built under the sink.
examples: The bathroom *vanity* has a cracked countertop.
She sat at the *vanity* doing her hair.
We're replacing both *vanities* next month.

gloss: A cloth bag filled with soft material that you rest your head on.
examples: This *pillow* is completely flat.
He sleeps with three *pillows*.
She cried into her *pillow*.

gloss: The removable cloth cover that slips over a pillow.
examples: Put a clean *pillowcase* on before your mother gets here.
The *pillowcases* don't match the sheets.
He used a *pillowcase* to carry his laundry.

gloss: A large piece of thick cloth used to keep warm in bed.
examples: Grab an extra *blanket* — it's freezing tonight.
There are wool *blankets* in the hall closet.
She wrapped a *blanket* around her shoulders.
contrast: The *n* before *k* is pronounced /ŋ/, so it sounds like BLANG-kit, not BLAN-kit.

gloss: A thick bed cover made of two layers stitched together with padding between.
examples: My grandmother made this *quilt* by hand.
The *quilts* hanging on the wall are all family heirlooms.
He pulled the *quilt* up to his chin.

gloss: A thick padded bed cover, usually filled with down or synthetic fiber.
examples: The *comforter* barely fits in the washing machine.
We got a new *comforter* set on sale.
Down *comforters* are warm but expensive.
contrast: American *comforter* is roughly the British *duvet* — and Americans sell duvets separately, as a cover.

gloss: A soft quilt filled with down, used with a removable cover.
examples: The *duvet* cover is in the wash.
She shook out the *duvet* and remade the bed.
Hotel *duvets* are always too hot for me.
contrast: A French borrowing: the final *t* is silent and the stress falls on the second syllable — doo-VAY.

gloss: A decorative cover laid over a made bed.
examples: The motel *bedspread* had seen better days.
She smoothed the *bedspread* and stepped back.
All the *bedspreads* in the catalog were beige.

gloss: Sheets, blankets, and pillows taken together.
examples: Bring your own *bedding* if you're staying over.
All the *bedding* needs to be washed after the trip.
The camp provides cots but no *bedding*.
contrast: Uncountable: *some bedding*, *a lot of bedding* — never *a bedding* or *beddings*.

gloss: Cloth woven from flax, or the household cloth goods made from it.
examples: The tablecloth is heavy *linen*.
Fresh *linen* is stored in the hall closet.
He wore a rumpled *linen* jacket.

gloss: A piece of furniture with doors and shelves for storing things.
examples: The glasses are in the *cabinet* above the sink.
We're painting the kitchen *cabinets* white.
He keeps his tools in a locked *cabinet* in the garage.

gloss: A cabinet with shelves for dishes or food.
examples: The *cupboard* was bare except for a can of soup.
She reached into the *cupboard* for a mug.
All the *cupboards* stick in humid weather.
contrast: The *p* is silent and the vowel is short: KUB-urd, not KUP-bord.

gloss: A small storage room or recess in a wall, usually for clothes.
examples: Hang your coat in the hall *closet*.
This apartment has almost no *closet* space.
The bedroom *closets* are surprisingly deep.
contrast: First vowel is /ɑː/ as in *hot*, not the /oʊ/ of *close*: KLAH-zut.

gloss: A sliding box that pulls out of a piece of furniture.
examples: The scissors are in the junk *drawer*.
This *drawer* sticks every time.
He emptied all the *drawers* into a box.
contrast: One syllable for most Americans — it sounds like *draw* plus an r, not DRAW-er.

gloss: A piece of furniture with shelves for books.
examples: The *bookcase* runs the whole length of the wall.
We anchored the *bookcases* so they can't tip over.
There's a *bookcase* in every room of that house.

gloss: A large sturdy box with a lid, used for storage.
examples: The blankets are in the cedar *chest*.
They dragged two heavy *chests* down from the attic.
She keeps her mother's letters in a small wooden *chest*.

gloss: A large reinforced case or box for storing or carrying belongings.
examples: Her old costumes are in a *trunk* in the basement.
The attic was full of dusty *trunks*.
He sat on the *trunk* to get the lid to close.

gloss: A tall narrow cupboard that locks, used in schools and gyms.
examples: My books are still in my *locker*.
The *lockers* line both sides of the hallway.
You need a quarter to use the *locker* at the pool.

gloss: A small room or closet where food and supplies are kept.
examples: There's another bag of flour in the *pantry*.
Our new place has a walk-in *pantry*.
Both *pantries* were stocked for the winter.

gloss: A long low cabinet in a dining room for dishes and linens.
examples: The good china lives in the *sideboard*.
She set the desserts out on the *sideboard*.
Old *sideboards* are heavy as anything.

gloss: A frame with bars or shelves for holding or hanging things.
examples: Hang the towel on the *rack*.
The store had a whole *rack* of winter coats on sale.
We put shoe *racks* in both closets.

gloss: Shelves considered together, or the material they are made from.
examples: We put up metal *shelving* along the garage wall.
The basement needs more *shelving*.
Adjustable *shelving* costs a little more but it's worth it.
contrast: Uncountable, unlike the countable *shelf*: *a lot of shelving*, never *a shelving*.

gloss: A container woven from cane, wire, or plastic strips.
examples: Toss the mail in the *basket* by the door.
She lines the *baskets* with cloth napkins.
There's a wicker *basket* under the bench for hats and gloves.

gloss: A tall lidded basket for dirty laundry.
examples: Put your shirt in the *hamper*, not on the floor.
The *hamper* is overflowing again.
We keep separate *hampers* for darks and whites.
contrast: In American English a *hamper* holds dirty laundry; in British English it's a basket of food given as a gift.

gloss: A deep container for storing or sorting things.
examples: The winter clothes are in a plastic *bin* in the attic.
Label the *bins* so we know what's in them.
He dumped the toys into the storage *bin*.
contrast: In the US a *bin* is a storage container; in British English *the bin* means the trash can.

gloss: A shaped frame with a hook that a garment hangs from.
examples: There aren't enough *hangers* in this closet.
Put your jacket on a *hanger* so it doesn't wrinkle.
The dry cleaner gave everything back on wire *hangers*.
contrast: No /ɡ/ sound: it rhymes with *banger*, not with *finger*.

gloss: A curved piece of metal or plastic for hanging things on.
examples: Your keys are on the *hook* by the door.
We screwed a row of *hooks* into the wall for backpacks.
The robe hangs on a *hook* behind the bathroom door.

gloss: A small container for paper and other dry trash.
examples: He crumpled the letter and tossed it in the *wastebasket*.
Every office has a *wastebasket* under the desk.
The cleaners empty the *wastebaskets* at night.

gloss: A hanging piece of cloth that covers a window.
examples: Close the *curtains* — the sun's right in my eyes.
She sewed a *curtain* for the kitchen window.
The shower *curtain* needs replacing.

gloss: Heavy lined curtains that hang to the floor.
examples: The *drapes* in the dining room block out all the light.
They had the *drapes* custom made.
Velvet *drapes* collect an incredible amount of dust.
contrast: Nearly always plural in American English; the singular *drape* for one panel is rare in speech.

gloss: A window covering of slats or a roll of stiff material.
examples: Can you open the *blinds*? It's dark in here.
One slat on the *blind* is bent.
We put wooden *blinds* in the living room.
contrast: Same spelling as the adjective *blind*, and usually spoken of in the plural: *the blinds*.

gloss: A hinged panel that covers a window from inside or outside.
examples: One *shutter* is hanging by a single hinge.
They painted the *shutters* dark green.
We closed the *shutters* before the storm.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A thick woven floor covering, often fitted wall to wall.
examples: We're pulling up the old *carpet* and refinishing the floors.
There's a stain on the *carpet* in the hallway.
Persian *carpets* like that don't come cheap.
contrast: Fitted floor covering is uncountable in the US — *new carpet*, *wall-to-wall carpet* — while a loose piece is usually called a *rug*.

gloss: A loose piece of thick fabric covering part of a floor.
examples: The *rug* keeps sliding around on the wood floor.
She bought two matching *rugs* for the bedroom.
Just sweep it under the *rug* — nobody will notice.

gloss: A small flat piece of material placed on the floor for a specific purpose.
examples: Wipe your feet on the *mat*.
We keep a rubber *mat* in front of the sink.
The bath *mats* are in the linen closet.

gloss: A rough mat outside a door for cleaning your shoes.
examples: The spare key is not under the *doormat* — that's the first place people look.
Our *doormat* says GO AWAY, which the neighbors find hilarious.
They sell those *doormats* at the hardware store.

gloss: A cloth spread over a table before a meal.
examples: Somebody spilled red wine on the white *tablecloth*.
She irons the *tablecloth* before every holiday.
The *tablecloths* are folded in the bottom drawer.

gloss: A square of cloth or paper used at a meal to wipe your hands and mouth.
examples: Can you grab me a *napkin*? I spilled.
He wrote the whole plan on a *napkin*.
The cloth *napkins* only come out at Thanksgiving.

gloss: A small mat set under each person's plate at the table.
examples: Set a *placemat* at every seat.
The vinyl *placemats* wipe clean in a second.
She made a *placemat* out of scrap fabric.

gloss: A small disc placed under a glass to protect a table.
examples: Use a *coaster* — that table marks easily.
The bar gave out cardboard *coasters* with the logo on them.
Her drink left a ring because she ignored the *coaster*.

gloss: A piece of absorbent cloth for drying yourself or something else.
examples: There's a clean *towel* in the bathroom for you.
The beach *towels* are still in the car.
He dried his hands on a dish *towel*.
contrast: Two syllables, rhyming with *vowel*; keep it distinct from *tower*, which ends in an r sound.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: Cloth made by weaving or knitting.
examples: We picked a heavy *fabric* for the curtains.
The store carries upholstery *fabrics* by the yard.
That *fabric* wrinkles if you look at it wrong.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: Woven material, or a small piece of it used for cleaning.
examples: Wipe the counter with a damp *cloth*.
The chair is covered in coarse brown *cloth*.
Keep a few clean *cloths* under the sink.
contrast: Ends in the voiceless /θ/ and the plural is *cloths* — quite different from *clothes*, which sounds like *close*.

gloss: The padding and fabric covering a piece of soft furniture.
examples: The *upholstery* on that chair is worn through at the arms.
Leather *upholstery* costs extra.
He does *upholstery* work out of his garage.
contrast: Four syllables with the stress on the second — up-HOHL-stuh-ree, not UP-hol-stry.

gloss: A device holding a bulb that gives light in a room.
examples: Turn on the *lamp* — you'll ruin your eyes.
There's a reading *lamp* beside the bed.
Both *lamps* in the living room need new bulbs.

gloss: The cover over a bulb that softens or directs the light.
examples: The cat knocked the *lampshade* crooked again.
A paper *lampshade* yellows over time.
They sell replacement *lampshades* at the hardware store.

gloss: A large branched light fixture that hangs from the ceiling.
examples: A crystal *chandelier* hangs over the dining table.
Cleaning the *chandelier* takes half a day.
The lobby had two enormous *chandeliers*.
contrast: The *ch* is said /ʃ/ like *sh*, and the stress lands on the last syllable: shan-duh-LEER.

gloss: The glass part of a lamp that produces light.
examples: The *bulb* in the hallway burned out.
We switched all the *bulbs* over to LEDs.
Get a sixty-watt *bulb* while you're at the store.

gloss: The small control on a wall that turns a light on and off.
examples: The *switch* is on your left as you walk in.
Somebody painted right over the light *switch*.
There are three *switches* by the door and I never know which is which.

gloss: The point in a wall where you plug in an electrical device.
examples: Is there an *outlet* behind the couch?
This room only has two *outlets*.
Don't overload the *outlet* with all those cords.
contrast: American *outlet* is British *socket* or *power point*.

gloss: Something attached permanently to a building, such as a light or a sink.
examples: The ceiling *fixture* is original to the house.
We replaced all the bathroom *fixtures*.
The price includes the appliances but not the light *fixtures*.

gloss: A piece of glass with a backing that reflects what is in front of it.
examples: There's a full-length *mirror* on the closet door.
She checked her hair in the *mirror* one more time.
The gym has *mirrors* on every wall.
contrast: Two syllables, both r sounds pronounced: MIH-rur, not MEER.

gloss: A container for holding cut flowers.
examples: Put the roses in a *vase* before they wilt.
He knocked over the *vase* reaching for the remote.
The shelf is lined with little glass *vases*.
contrast: Americans say VAYSS, rhyming with *face*; the British say VAHZ.

gloss: The border that holds a picture or mirror.
examples: The photo came in a cheap plastic *frame*.
We had the drawing put in a proper *frame*.
There are family pictures in silver *frames* along the mantel.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: A picture made with paint, or the art of making such pictures.
examples: There's a big *painting* of the coast over the fireplace.
She sold three *paintings* at the fair.
He took up *painting* after he retired.

gloss: A painting, drawing, or photograph, especially one hung on a wall.
examples: That *picture* has been crooked for a year.
The hallway is covered in *pictures* of the grandkids.
He hung a *picture* to cover the hole in the plaster.
contrast: PIK-chur — do not confuse it with *pitcher* (PICH-ur), the jug you pour from.

gloss: A large printed sheet put on a wall for decoration or advertising.
examples: He still has a band *poster* from high school on his wall.
The *posters* were held up with tape and prayer.
She framed a movie *poster* for the hallway.

gloss: A device that shows the time, standing on a surface or hung on a wall.
examples: The kitchen *clock* runs five minutes fast.
We had to reset all the *clocks* after the power went out.
There's an old grandfather *clock* in the hall.
contrast: A *clock* stands or hangs; the one you wear is a *watch*. Countable, unlike Russian *часы*: *a clock*, *two clocks*.

gloss: A stick of wax with a wick, burned for light or scent.
examples: Light a *candle* — the power's out.
She burns scented *candles* in the bathroom.
The *candle* dripped wax all over the tablecloth.

gloss: A holder with a socket for one candle.
examples: A brass *candlestick* sat at each end of the table.
The silver *candlesticks* only come out for company.
She polished the *candlestick* until it gleamed.

gloss: A small decorative object, especially one hung on a Christmas tree.
examples: One glass *ornament* broke on the way down from the attic.
The tree is loaded with homemade *ornaments*.
She keeps each *ornament* wrapped in tissue paper.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: An object added to make a place look nicer, or the act of decorating.
examples: The *decorations* stay up until after New Year's.
That vase is just *decoration* — nobody puts flowers in it.
We hung one *decoration* in every window.

gloss: Decorative paper pasted onto the walls of a room.
examples: The *wallpaper* in the hallway is peeling at the seams.
We stripped all the old *wallpaper* off before painting.
That striped *wallpaper* makes the ceiling look higher.
contrast: Uncountable in English even though Russian *обои* is plural: *some wallpaper*, *a roll of wallpaper* — never *wallpapers*.

gloss: The overall style and furnishings of a room.
examples: The *decor* hasn't changed since the seventies.
She has a real eye for *decor*.
The restaurant's *decor* is all dark wood and brass.
contrast: A French borrowing with the stress on the second syllable — day-KOR, not DAY-kor.

gloss: An old object valued for its age and craftsmanship.
examples: That desk is a genuine *antique*.
They sell *antiques* out of a barn off the highway.
Half the furniture in the house is an *antique* of some kind.
contrast: Stress on the second syllable and *-que* is just /k/: an-TEEK, not AN-tikw.

gloss: The furniture, curtains, and fittings that make up a room.
examples: The apartment comes with all the *furnishings*.
They spent more on *furnishings* than on the car.
The *furnishings* were sold off piece by piece.
contrast: Always plural and takes a plural verb: *the furnishings are*, never *a furnishing*.

gloss: The part of a door, drawer, or pot that you take hold of.
examples: The *handle* on the fridge came loose.
We swapped out all the drawer *handles* for brass ones.
Push down on the *handle* and pull.

gloss: A round handle you turn or pull.
examples: The *knob* on the oven is missing.
New cabinet *knobs* can change the whole look of a kitchen.
He turned the *knob* slowly so it wouldn't creak.
contrast: The *k* is silent, as in *knife* and *knee*: NAHB.

gloss: The round handle used to open a door.
examples: The *doorknob* on the bathroom sticks.
He hung the sign on the *doorknob*.
The old house still has its original glass *doorknobs*.

gloss: The jointed metal fitting a door or lid swings on.
examples: That *hinge* needs a drop of oil.
The cabinet door is off its *hinges*.
He tightened every *hinge* in the house one Saturday.

gloss: A simple fastening that holds a door, gate, or lid shut.
examples: Make sure the *latch* catches or the gate blows open.
The *latch* on the toolbox is broken.
Childproof *latches* went on every low cabinet.

gloss: A device that keeps a door or container shut until it is opened with a key or code.
examples: The *lock* on the back door sticks in cold weather.
We changed the *locks* after we moved in.
There's a *lock* on the liquor cabinet for a reason.

gloss: A pointed metal fastener with a spiral thread, turned with a screwdriver.
examples: One *screw* is missing from the shelf bracket.
The bookcase came with a bag of *screws* and no instructions.
Don't overtighten the *screw* or you'll strip the wood.

gloss: A thin pointed metal pin hammered into wood or a wall.
examples: Hang the picture on that *nail*.
There are still *nails* sticking out of the old boards.
He hit the *nail* crooked and had to pull it out.

gloss: The metal fittings of furniture and buildings — handles, hinges, screws, and locks.
examples: The dresser is solid, but the *hardware* is cheap.
We picked up some *hardware* at the store on the corner.
All the *hardware* in the kitchen is brushed nickel.
contrast: Uncountable: *some hardware*, *a piece of hardware* — never *a hardware* or *hardwares*.

gloss: A long thin bar, especially the one a curtain hangs from.
examples: The curtain *rod* pulled right out of the drywall.
We need a longer *rod* for that window.
Both closet *rods* are sagging under all those clothes.

gloss: A barrier of bars along stairs, a balcony, or a porch.
examples: Hold the *railing* — those steps are icy.
The porch *railing* needs to be repainted.
The iron *railings* rusted through at the base.

gloss: The handrail along the side of a staircase.
examples: As a kid he slid down the *banister* every morning.
The *banister* is loose at the top of the stairs.
They stripped and stained the *banister* by hand.

gloss: A shaped strip of wood or plaster running along a wall or ceiling as trim.
examples: The crown *molding* is what sold us on the house.
They matched the new *molding* to the original.
All the *moldings* were painted over about six times.
contrast: American spelling *molding*; the British write *moulding*, with the same pronunciation.

gloss: The narrow board running along the bottom of a wall where it meets the floor.
examples: The *baseboard* is scuffed all along the hallway.
Wipe down the *baseboards* before the showing.
We ran the cable behind the *baseboard*.
contrast: American *baseboard* is British *skirting board*.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A flat piece of baked clay or stone used to cover a floor or wall.
examples: One *tile* by the tub is cracked.
The kitchen floor is *tile*, not wood.
They laid the *tiles* in a herringbone pattern.

gloss: A fixed basin with a faucet and a drain.
examples: There are dishes piled in the *sink* again.
The bathroom has two *sinks*, which ended a lot of arguments.
The *sink* is draining slowly.

gloss: The fitting you turn to let water out of a pipe.
examples: The kitchen *faucet* drips all night.
Turn the *faucet* off all the way.
We replaced both bathroom *faucets* last spring.
contrast: American *faucet* is British *tap*.

gloss: The large fixed basin you sit in to wash.
examples: The kids are in the *bathtub*.
That old cast-iron *bathtub* weighs a ton.
Some of the newer units don't even have *bathtubs*.
contrast: Americans say *bathtub* or just *tub*; the British call it a *bath*, which in the US means the act of washing.

gloss: The seated fixture used for waste, with a bowl and a flush.
examples: The *toilet* keeps running after you flush.
He dropped his phone in the *toilet*.
The stadium has about forty *toilets* and they're all occupied.
contrast: In the US *toilet* means the fixture only; the room is a *bathroom* or, in public, a *restroom*.

gloss: A fixture that sprays water over you, or the enclosure it is in.
examples: The *shower* has no water pressure at all.
There's mildew in the corner of the *shower*.
The gym *showers* are open until ten.

gloss: A metal unit that heats a room with hot water or steam.
examples: The *radiator* clanks all night in the winter.
She dried her mittens on the *radiator*.
The old *radiators* were painted the same color as the walls.
contrast: Stress falls on the first syllable — RAY-dee-ay-tur — not on the second as in Russian *радиатор*.

gloss: An opening in a wall where a fire is built, with a chimney above it.
examples: We hung the stockings over the *fireplace*.
The house has *fireplaces* in three rooms.
The *fireplace* is gas now, but it used to burn wood.

gloss: The shelf above a fireplace.
examples: The photos are lined up along the *mantel*.
He set his keys on the *mantel* and forgot them there.
Both *mantels* are carved oak.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *mantle*, the cloak or the layer of the earth — same pronunciation, different word.

gloss: The flat work surface on top of kitchen or bathroom cabinets.
examples: The granite *countertop* is cold in the morning.
Wipe down the *countertops* before you go.
There's not much *countertop* space in this kitchen.
contrast: American *countertop* is British *worktop*.

gloss: A machine used in the home, such as a refrigerator or a washing machine.
examples: The rent includes all the *appliances*.
One *appliance* after another broke that year.
Stainless steel *appliances* show every fingerprint.
contrast: Countable in English, unlike the Russian mass noun *техника*: *an appliance*, *three appliances*.
